title: Pakistan Faces Pressure on Four Fronts as Balochistan, Houthis, and Afghan Border Crises Converge
excerpt: From a Baloch insurgency threatening Chinese mines to Houthi attacks risking military entanglement with Saudi Arabia, Pakistan confronts simultaneous security challenges that could reshape the region.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Pakistan faces multiple crises: Baloch insurgency, Houthi conflict risk, Afghan tensions, and economic strain.
  • 42 people were killed in July due to Balochistan violence, prompting military operations.
  • Saindak copper-gold mine may halt production due to security issues affecting Chinese investments.
  • Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia threaten Pakistan's military involvement under a defense pact.
  • India's diplomatic mission in Kabul adds complexity to Pakistan's security challenges.

  • Pakistan faces simultaneous crises: a deadly Baloch insurgency that killed 42 people in July, the risk of being drawn into a Saudi-Houthi conflict, escalating Afghan border tensions, and an economy squeezed by energy disruptions.
  • The Saindak copper-gold mine in Balochistan warned it could halt production within a month due to worsening militant violence, threatening Chinese investment.
  • Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia have pushed Islamabad to the brink — Pakistani troops are deployed near the Saudi-Yemen border under a mutual defence pact.
  • India's reopening of a full diplomatic mission in Kabul adds a strategic dimension to Pakistan's multi-front challenge.

Pakistan is navigating its most complex security landscape in years, facing simultaneous pressures from a resurgent Baloch insurgency, the risk of military entanglement in the Saudi-Houthi conflict, an unresolved confrontation with Afghanistan, and an economy battered by energy shortages linked to the US-Iran war.

Balochistan: Insurgency Threatens Chinese Investment

In early July, coordinated attacks by the Balochistan Liberation Army (BLA) and the Pakistani Taliban (TTP) across multiple districts in Balochistan killed 42 people, including 38 security personnel. The Pakistan Armed Forces responded with Operation Shaban, a multi-district counter-insurgency campaign that has killed 129 militants as of July 16, according to military statements.

The violence has put major Chinese-backed projects at risk. Saindak Metals Limited, the joint venture behind Pakistan's largest operating copper and gold mine, warned the energy ministry that operations could become "unsustainable within a month" because deteriorating security was disrupting supply routes, according to the Financial Times. The mine, operated by the state-owned Metallurgical Corporation of China, exports most of its output to China.

"We have directed the provincial authorities and all concerned security agencies to beef up deployment for all of their installations, personnel, logistics and transportation."

— Talal Chaudhry, Pakistan's state minister for the interior

The unrest has also clouded the outlook for Barrick Mining's $9 billion Reko Diq gold and copper project, located just 50 kilometres from Saindak. Baloch separatists have sought an independent state for decades, arguing that Pakistan and foreign allies have exploited the province's natural resources without adequately benefiting local communities.

Houthis and Saudi Arabia: Pakistan's Red Line

The second front is the Middle East. Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia this week pierced a four-year truce and have frustrated Islamabad, which signed a mutual defence agreement with Riyadh last year and has deployed thousands of soldiers and a squadron of fighter jets to the kingdom.

"Our top civil and military leaders have conveyed to Iran at the highest level that the attacks on Saudi Arabia are attacks on Pakistan," a Pakistani official told Reuters. "It is our red line."

Pakistani soldiers are stationed near the Saudi border with Yemen, two Pakistani officials said, increasing their direct exposure. A widening Houthi campaign could force Pakistan to intervene militarily under the terms of its defence pact — a scenario Islamabad has so far tried to avoid through mediation between Washington and Tehran.

Middle East Tensions: A Red Line
›Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia threaten Pakistan's security.
›Thousands of Pakistani troops deployed near Saudi border.
›Mutual defense pact with Saudi Arabia signed last year.
›Pakistan warns attacks on Saudi are attacks on itself.

Retired Pakistani general Ghulam Mustafa cautioned that while "Pakistan's top leaders are still engaged in appeasing all stakeholders," this could change "if the Houthis expand the radius of their attacks in Saudi Arabia."

Afghanistan: The Unresolved Western Border

The third front is Afghanistan. Talks between the two countries collapsed in late 2025 after three rounds of Qatar- and Turkiye-mediated negotiations broke down. Pakistan accuses the Taliban of harbouring TTP militants; Kabul denies the charge. In February 2026, Pakistan's defence minister declared "open war" on Afghanistan, and Operation Ghazab Lil Haq struck Taliban military installations, not just militant camps, according to East Asia Forum.

India's reopening of a full diplomatic mission in Kabul and public commitments of medical and development aid add a strategic complication. Pakistan now faces what analysts call a "two-front" problem: rivalry with India to the east and a volatile Afghan border to the west.

The Economic Squeeze

Economic Strain Amid Security Crises
›Inflation reached 10.9% in April 2026.
›Emergency measures imposed to manage fuel shortages.
›US-Iran tensions disrupt oil and gas supply routes.
›Government struggles with rising food and electricity costs.

Underlying all three security challenges is economic fragility. Tensions around the Strait of Hormuz linked to the US-Iran war have disrupted Pakistan's oil and gas supply routes. The government imposed emergency measures, including early business closures, to prevent fuel shortages. Inflation hit 10.9% in April 2026, squeezing households already struggling with food, fuel, and electricity costs.

Pakistan's mediation between Washington and Tehran has been as much about reopening these supply routes as about diplomatic prestige, according to analysts and officials. "Yes, there is frustration, but that doesn't mean that we are abandoning this project," one official told Reuters. "We have invested a lot in it, and we have an interest in keeping it afloat."
